1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: French Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6.background: One of Black's three main replies to 2.Nf3, with 2...d6 and 2...Nc6. After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 it leads to the Taimanov Variation, named after Mark Taimanov, and the Kan Variation, named after Ilya Kan and also called the Paulsen Variation after Louis Paulsen.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4.strategy: Offers the pawn trade that opens the game: after ...cxd4 White recaptures with a central knight and has open lines for both bishops and the queen, while Black gets a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file. White gets the initiative, Black the counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Delayed Alapin Variation, with e6
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3.strategy: Prepares to build a full pawn centre with d4 and to keep it there, a calmer way to meet the Sicilian than the open play after an immediate d4. The price is the c3 square for the b1-knight; Black can strike back in the centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: A waiting move: it develops, guards e4 and postpones d4 until Black shows which Sicilian it means to play. It mostly leads back into the usual open Sicilian, and the knight takes the square a c-pawn would want for a pawn centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c4.name: Sicilian Defence: Kramnik Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c4.strategy: Puts pawns on c4 and e4 so that d5 is covered twice, which holds back Black's freeing central break and gains space. White gives up the open play of d4 for a squeezing, positional game in which Black has to find room to breathe.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.b3.name: Sicilian Defence: French Variation, Westerinen Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.b3.background: It is a rare independent try, occasionally played by Heikki Westerinen in the 1970s.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and avoids the open Sicilian. It does nothing against Black's centre, though, and White's follow-up is unclear: Black is free to develop as it likes and to build a solid centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: Wing Gambit Deferred
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.b4.strategy: A gambit: White offers the b-pawn to pull Black's c-pawn away and build a big pawn centre with d4. Black can take the pawn safely, but White gets space and active play in return, so the move is playable though riskier than the usual third moves.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 before White's pawn centre exists. The tension is resolved at once, White cannot enjoy the broad centre that c3 was preparing, and Black's pieces come out freely in an open game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, so White must either advance the pawn, gaining space but leaving a target, or defend it. Black keeps its choice of centre set-up open and makes White decide what to do with the e-pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queenside knight and adds to the control of d4, so White's central pawn break meets resistance at once. It leaves e4 alone, though, so White can still build a broad centre, and Black must be ready to attack it with pieces and pawns afterwards.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Opens the centre at once: White trades the e-pawn for Black's d-pawn and, with c3 already supporting d4, can follow by planting a pawn on d4. Black must recapture and deal with an open game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.e5.strategy: Gains space, but it releases the tension in the centre and concedes the e4 square for good. Black can strike with ...d4 at once, attacking the c3-pawn before White's centre is built.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5+.strategy: Develops with check, but the gain is small: Black blocks with a developing move, and the d5-pawn still attacks the undefended e4-pawn, so White has to resolve the centre at once. The bishop may then have to trade itself or retreat.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 exd5.strategy: The natural recapture: the queen stays at home, the c8-bishop is freed and Black holds a broad centre of c5 and d5 pawns. Black must develop quickly, because White can challenge that centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which stands in the centre but can be harassed by White's developing moves. Black keeps the pawn structure intact; in the play that follows, White usually ends up with an isolated queen's pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Declines to recapture with a pawn and develops with an attack on d5, offering the pawn for time. White can simply take on e6 and, once Black recaptures, is a pawn up; Black's lead in development has to pay for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 exd5 5.B.strategy: Gives check before Black's pieces are out, so the bishop develops with a gain of time. If Black blocks with the knight it is pinned, and an exchange on c6 would double Black's pawns. White heads for castling and a central break.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 exd5 5.d.strategy: Claims the centre at once: the pawn, backed by c3 and the f3-knight, challenges c5 before Black's pieces are developed. If the c-pawns come off, the structure is symmetrical and White, with the move, keeps the initiative and the freer development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 exd5 5.B.strategy: A quiet developing move that prepares to castle. It does not challenge Black's pawns on c5 and d5, so Black can complete development without hurry and holds an equal game.

Blocks with a developing move that adds to the control of d4, where White wants to build the centre. The knight is pinned against the king for now, which Black accepts in return for natural, quick development.

Blocks with the bishop instead of the knight, so the b8-knight stays free to choose its square. If White trades on d7, Black recaptures with a developing move and the game is level; if White retreats, Black's bishop is already out.

Blocks with the b8-knight, which is then pinned against the king and shuts in the c8-bishop. If White trades on d7, Black gets the bishop pair, but the cramped development makes this a passive way to meet the check.
Puts the king in safety before the centre opens and keeps the pin on c6, so Black's knight stays tied. White completes development first and then takes the centre, leaving Black to untangle the pin.

Claims the centre at once and uses the pin on c6 to keep that knight from joining the fight for d4. The cost is that White has not yet castled, so if the centre opens the king in the middle needs care.

Gives up the bishop for the knight to damage Black's pawn structure, but Black recaptures with the b-pawn and gets the bishop pair and a half-open b-file in return. White must show that the doubled pawns are a real weakness; meanwhile Black's centre stays strong.

Develops the bishop on an open diagonal, supports the c5-pawn and prepares to castle. Black answers the pin with quick development and keeps the centre pawns together, aiming for a position in which both sides develop smoothly.

Develops the king's knight naturally, but lets White play Re1 with check at once, so Black has to spend a move on the king's safety while the pin on c6 stays. Sound, but White's pieces gain a little activity.
Puts the bishop on a safe square where it still guards c5 and prepares castling. It is solid but passive: the c6-knight stays pinned and Black does little to prepare for White's central break.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.d.strategy: Takes central space at once and attacks the c5-pawn, while Black's queen is out in the open. White's structure is sound and the pieces have natural squares, so White gets the easier development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.B.strategy: Develops the bishop to a square the queen cannot attack and prepares to castle; a bishop on c4 would simply hang to the queen. White keeps the d4 break in reserve with the pieces in place.

Develops with check, but the gain in time is small: Black blocks with a developing move, and the bishop must then trade itself for a knight or retreat. Meanwhile Black's queen stays comfortably placed in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.d.name: Sicilian Defence: Delayed Alapin Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.d.strategy: Develops a piece and defends the queen on d5, so Black can hold the c5-pawn and wait. The usual middlegame follows once the pawns are exchanged on d4, leaving White an isolated queen's pawn that must be paid for with active piece play.

Brings a third attacker to d4 (the c5-pawn, the queen and the knight), so White has to keep the pawn defended and cannot develop carelessly. The c3-pawn keeps the b1-knight from hitting the queen, which lets Black keep the tension instead of exchanging.

Exchanges at once and leaves White with an isolated queen's pawn after the recapture, which Black can aim at. The cost is that with the c-file open the b1-knight can come to c3 with a tempo on the queen, so Black spends time moving it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5.strategy: Drives the knight away and takes space, committing White to a pawn on e5 that Black will attack. If White's pieces can support it, the cramp on Black's kingside is a real asset; if not, the pawn is overextended.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Protects e4 with a pawn instead of advancing it, and frees the c1-bishop. White gives up the broad pawn centre for a slower game of piece play, and Black can develop freely and expand with ...d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.Qc2.strategy: Defends e4 with the queen, which keeps the d-pawn free to advance and the knights' squares open. It is an early queen move with no clear plan behind it, so Black develops freely and White's set-up stays modest.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, which has no better square, and eyes c3. The knight stands well here, and White's c3, played earlier, takes away the natural square of the b1-knight and so helps Black.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Ne4.strategy: Hits c3 and the centre, but d3 drives the knight away and it has no safe square: taking on c3 gives up a piece for a pawn, and every other retreat is covered by a White pawn or piece. The move simply loses a piece.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Ng4.strategy: Attacks the e5-pawn, but the f3-knight guards it, so there is no threat. h3 drives the knight to the edge of the board, and White builds the centre with tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 5.d4.strategy: Supports the e5-pawn and builds the centre, challenging the c5-pawn at the same time. White gains space and a firm hold on the centre, and Black has to attack the pawn chain to make use of the central knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 5.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop with pressure on the d5-knight, which only the e6-pawn guards, and prepares to castle, while the d4 break stays in reserve. The cost is time: Black can start undermining the e5-pawn before White's centre is built.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 5.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop and castle quickly, building on solid squares. It is slow: the bishop on g2 would be hemmed in by the f3-knight until that moves, and Black gets time to attack the e5-pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 5.d4.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Sherzer Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c3 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 5.d4.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d4, but d4 is well defended and White answers c4 at once, chasing the d5 knight away with a gain of time. White then has a broad pawn centre and more space, and Black's knight lands on a poor square.

The natural capture: it challenges the base of White's chain and opens the c-file, while the knight on d5 holds a strong post. Black can then play against the d4 and e5 pawns with pieces, but White keeps a spacious centre, so Black must hurry with development.

Strikes at the head of White's pawn chain at once, so White must decide whether to hold the space or exchange it away. The price is a tempo spent on a pawn move, and the e6-pawn can become a target once the centre opens.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4.name: Sicilian Defence: French Variation, Open
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: Trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn: Black gets a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file to work with. It costs time and hands White free development and open lines, the usual bargain of the open Sicilian.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 a6.name: Sicilian Defence: Drazic Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a6 before resolving the centre and prepares ...b5. Black has not yet taken on d4, so White can choose the pawn structure first.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 d5.name: Sicilian Defence: Marshall Counterattack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, but opens the game before Black is developed. White takes the pawn, and a check with the bishop gains time, so Black is the one defending against a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight takes the centre and the bishops and queen get open lines. It will be harassed by Black's developing moves, so White's piece set-up must be ready to meet them, but the central knight also supports a later attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Deferred
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.strategy: A gambit that offers a pawn for a lead in development and an open c-file. Black keeps a real extra pawn that White must justify by quick development, so the idea only works if White's pieces come out faster than Black can untangle.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which stands in the centre but can be hit at once: ...Nc6 attacks it with a gain of time and the queen has to go back. White's structure stays healthy, so the damage is a tempo, but it gives Black the easier development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 away from White's bishop and knights and prepares ...b5 for queenside space. Black waits to see whether White opens the centre with d4, in which case the play transposes into a normal Open Sicilian with the pawn already on a6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with control of d4 and e5 and puts off every decision about the other pieces. If White opens the centre, Black has a flexible set-up with a sound pawn structure and counterplay on the c-file, and the queenside advance with ...a6 and ...b5 stays available.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Builds the compact pair of pawns on d6 and e6, which guards e5 and c5 and leaves White's e4-e5 push without a hold. Black commits the d-pawn early and gives up the flexibility of waiting, trading some counterplay for a sturdy centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3.strategy: Heads for a fianchetto: the bishop on g2 will support e4 and watch the long diagonal. White does not hurry to open the centre and keeps d4 in reserve, which also sidesteps much of the sharpest Open Sicilian theory but gives Black time for the queenside advance.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once and heads for an Open Sicilian with the knight already developed on c3. White gets the usual lead in development and extra space, while Black's a6 has taken b5 away from the knights, so White plays for quick development and central control.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.Be2.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly and prepares castling, keeping the central break in reserve. It lets Black advance on the queenside without hindrance, and the bishop on e2 is less active than on d3 or g2, so White has not yet chosen a plan.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5.strategy: Advances on the queenside at once to gain space and prepare ...Bb7 against e4; the pawn is defended by a6, and ...b4 later chases the c3 knight. Black uses the slower g3 to start queenside play early.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with control of d4 and e5 and decides on the queenside advance later. Black treats the slow g3 as a reason to develop naturally; the cost is that the counterplay on the wing where a6 has already been prepared starts more slowly.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once and tries to profit from White's slow g3. After the exchange Black has a pawn pair on c5 and d5 and an open e-file, but the king is still in the centre and the pawns can become targets once White breaks with d4.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once, before Black's queenside advance gets going. After the exchange White's knight settles on d4 with the bishop on g2 to come, supporting e4, and White has an Open Sicilian in which Black's queenside pawns have already advanced.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto before opening the centre: once the f3 knight moves, the bishop backs e4 and watches the long diagonal. White keeps the central break in reserve and lets Black's queenside advance run on, ready to meet it from a solid set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.a4.strategy: Challenges the b5 pawn at once, before the queenside expansion gains more space. Black can push on with ...b4 and drive the knight back, or trade on a4; either way White has spent a tempo on a wing pawn while the centre is still unsettled.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.d4 c.strategy: Takes the central pawn, opening the c-file for Black's rook and removing White's chance to build a broad centre. Ignoring the challenge would let White decide how to resolve the tension, so Black captures at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.d4 B.strategy: Develops the bishop against e4 but leaves the central tension unresolved. White decides whether to take on c5 or push on with d5, and Black gives up the open c-file that capturing on d4 would bring in exchange for quicker development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.d4 N.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d4, but leaves the tension in the centre to White. The reply d5 attacks the c6 knight with a gain of time, and White ends up with more space while Black's knight lands on a poor square.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 a6 4.g3 b5 5.d4 c.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which settles in the centre where it eyes e6, b5 and c6, and keeps the queen out of the reach of ...Nc6. The result is an Open Sicilian with Black's queenside pawns advanced and White's fianchetto set-up, so both sides play on the queenside.

Recaptures with the queen, which regains the pawn but walks into ...Nc6 with a gain of time, so the queen has to move again. White achieves nothing the knight recapture would not, and Black develops easily.

Retreats the knight and leaves e4 without a defender: ...Bb7 hits the pawn at once, and ...Bb4+ gains a tempo. White can win the d4 pawn back, but only after Black has seized the initiative, so the knight recapture is clearly better.
